Abstract


Coparenting,

as

a

central

element

of

family

functioning,

constitutes

an

important

family

subsystem

for

an

ecological

understanding

of

digital

media

use

in

childhood.

This

study

aimed

to

explore

how

coparenting

processes

are

articulated

with

the

family

media

ecology

in

families

with

young

children,

seeking

to

understand

children’s

digital

media

use.

A

multiple

case

study

was

conducted

with

four

parental

dyads

with

children

up

to

four

years

of

age.

Abductive

thematic

analysis

was

guided

by

the

Ecological

Model

of

Coparenting

and

contemporary

frameworks

on

the

family

media

ecology.

Results

indicated

that

coparental

management

of

digital

media

use

is

integrated

into

basic

caregiving

routines

and

reflects

the

general

division

of

parental

tasks.

The

presence

of

tacit

consensus

between

caregivers

was

identified,

characterized

by

implicit

agreements

and

limited

structuring

of

rules

regarding

digital

media,

accompanied

by

situational

practices

and

greater

maternal

effort

in

everyday

media

management.

In

contrast,

contexts

marked

by

explicit

communication,

clear

rules,

and

shared

parental

responsibility

were

associated

with

more

predictable

and

consistent

practices.

Findings

also

revealed

reports

of

children’s

active

participation

in

the

family

media

ecology,

influencing

parental

decisions.

Understanding

digital

media

use

in

early

childhood

requires

considering

coparenting

and

the

child

as

inseparable

parts

of

the

family

ecology.

Strategies

to

promote

children’s

digital

health

should

foster

clear

parental

communication,

structured

routines,

and

support

for

shared

parental

responsibility

in

response

to

the

demands

of

a

digital

world.

Abstract


Coparenting,

as

a

central

element

of

family

functioning,

constitutes

an

important

family

subsystem

for

an

ecological

understanding

of

digital

media

use

in

childhood.

This

study

aimed

to

explore

how

coparenting

processes

are

articulated

with

the

family

media

ecology

in

families

with

young

children,

seeking

to

understand

children’s

digital

media

use.

A

multiple

case

study

was

conducted

with

four

parental

dyads

with

children

up

to

four

years

of

age.

Abductive

thematic

analysis

was

guided

by

the

Ecological

Model

of

Coparenting

and

contemporary

frameworks

on

the

family

media

ecology.

Results

indicated

that

coparental

management

of

digital

media

use

is

integrated

into

basic

caregiving

routines

and

reflects

the

general

division

of

parental

tasks.

The

presence

of

tacit

consensus

between

caregivers

was

identified,

characterized

by

implicit

agreements

and

limited

structuring

of

rules

regarding

digital

media,

accompanied

by

situational

practices

and

greater

maternal

effort

in

everyday

media

management.

In

contrast,

contexts

marked

by

explicit

communication,

clear

rules,

and

shared

parental

responsibility

were

associated

with

more

predictable

and

consistent

practices.

Findings

also

revealed

reports

of

children’s

active

participation

in

the

family

media

ecology,

influencing

parental

decisions.

Understanding

digital

media

use

in

early

childhood

requires

considering

coparenting

and

the

child

as

inseparable

parts

of

the

family

ecology.

Strategies

to

promote

children’s

digital

health

should

foster

clear

parental

communication,

structured

routines,

and

support

for

shared

parental

responsibility

in

response

to

the

demands

of

a

digital

world.

ecology;
